tagline: Up the western slope, where lumber once rode a flume.
intro: Out of Clovis, Highway 168 leaves the San Joaquin Valley for the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, passing Prather before climbing toward Shaver Lake and Huntington Lake. The road was once imagined as a crossing to the eastern Sierra. That connection was never built.
Clovis and Shaver Lake were joined by a different kind of route: a flume that carried lumber downhill to the railroad town. Water did the hauling. The lake later went to Southern California Edison.

moments.title: Clovis
moments.text: Clovis grew around a railroad stop and a lumber operation whose rough-cut boards arrived by water in a V-shaped flume.

moments.title: Prather
moments.text: At Prather, named for the rancher whose land became the town, Highway 168 is still below the climb toward the mountain lakes.

moments.title: Shaver Lake
moments.text: At 5,500 feet Shaver Lake once held timber for the flume company's mill, and most of its water now goes on to Big Creek to turn several powerhouses in succession.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service, Sierra National Forest scenic drives
